doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

title: Leading the band and turning down outside projects
summary: Fleck says leadership means accommodating everyone's solo work. After a previous bandleader's discomfort he refused outside projects, then learned the others did not mind and he should take care of himself too.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: As a leader of a group, do you ever have to make difficult decisions that make your bandmates unhappy?

Once in a while, although everybody is really good. They really understand because they all lead themselves. They all have their own groups and situations that they have to make those kinds of decisions about and I think that they are pretty cool with most things. Usually everything is about accommodation. That’s what the challenges are. Victor wants this time to do something. I’ve got a call to do this. Jeff might have this. Future Man might have this. But we have to work enough to keep this great crew that we have. We have these great guys that work with us that we’ve kept. Everyone who’s ever come to work with us has stayed and so if we’re all doing too many solo projects, I mean they’re all great, fun things to do but you know there’s also that feeling of responsibility to everybody. So generally the decisions that get made are always based on trying to take care of everybody in a situation so that it can have longevity. I was in a band where the leader was very uncomfortable with the people’s solo work and he would become very uncomfortable and so I learned, and I was burgeoning with my own ideas and they didn’t fit into the group and so I leaned from that, that even if it’s uncomfortable to not try to control what people did. And for a long time I controlled what I did but I’d let everybody else do what they wanted but I couldn’t do anything but the group. Because I felt like I was the name that people knew and I needed to send a real clear message that this is what I was doing. And I turned down a lot of cool things. And I always thought the other guys in the band, which had given up their whole other lives to be in this group that was largely my group, that I owed it to them to make that kind of commitment to them. They never seemed to actually feel that way. I discovered that they didn’t mind if I did outside stuff at all. But I didn’t feel like I should and so at a certain point I started to resent that

everybody in the group could get to do cool stuff outside the group but me, who had all these great opportunities I was turning down all the time. But I never talked to them about it. It was just something that was going on in my own head and gradually I realized that I had to take care of myself too, that I had to be part of the equation of making everybody happy. It wasn’t just everybody else but me. It was me too. And that it turned out to not be an issue. Everybody is happy, like they were really happy when they heard the records that I did on my own, the bluegrass records or the classical records, or the things with Edgar [Meyer]. I think they like that I’m doing that kind of stuff.
